messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Re: State-dependent diversification
parts:
Again none that I am aware of.  The issue is a bit more complex, as one is dealing with highly multivariate data. Thus, treating these data as a set of independent variables analyzed sequentially is not correct, and will not arrive at an appropriate answer. Also, one should be aware that in general, multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods that use parametric likelihood approaches have very high model misspecification, which increases as the dimensionality of the data becomes more highly multivariate. We’ve got a paper demonstrating these issues that one may wish to check out (Adams and Collyer, 2018, Syst. Biol.).  You can find this on my web page.

 

Dean

messages.author: 2fc03d53bc863e8d
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: State-dependent diversification
parts: It is possible to examine the relationship between phenotypic divergence and diversification rates, but not by the methods that you mentioned in your question (the methods for testing hypotheses about "state"-dependent diversification). Those methods relate discrete states to rates of diversification.  For examples of studies analyzing rates of phenotypic divergence to rates of diversification, see Rabosky, D. L. and D. C. Adams. 2012. Rates of morphological evolution are correlated with species richness in salamanders. Evolution 66:1807-1818 and Zelditch, M. L., J. Li, L. A. P. Tran, and D. L. Swiderski. 2015. Relationships of diversity, disparity and their evolutionary rates in squirrels (Sciuridae). Evolution 69:1284–1300. Now, in our analysis of squirrels, we used methods that are among those criticized by Adams and Collyer (2018) but the model that is implemented for shape (Brownian Motion) gave grossly inaccurate estimates of disparity: simulating the data using the parameters of that model, the predicted disparity was twice the  observed value, rather than the 2-5% too high/low (that we obtained by simulating the data under the models we used for estimating "rates").  If you do plan to use likelihood-based methods (mvMORPH), I'd recommend using parametric bootstrapping when selecting a model, and assessing the model-misspecification rates, which can be distressingly high.  The more serious problem for relating rates of phenotypic divergence to rates of diversification is that evolutionary"rates" are model-dependent so if different clades evolve by different modes, their rates are incommensurate.

messages.author: 2fc03d53bc863e8d
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: State-dependent diversification
parts: Yes, QuaSSE is for quantitative traits. An alternative, which ought to be adaptable to multidimensional data is in Harvey, M. G., D. L. Rabosky, and N. Cooper. 2018. Continuous traits and speciation rates: Alternatives to state-dependent diversification models. Methods Ecol. Evol. 9:984-993. This uses either PGLS or simulations to test for a relationship between tip-specific speciation rates and trait evolution. The problem is that you need a model for trait evolution (whether you use PGLS or simulations given parameters of the model).
